technique: time — how the poem moves through it, or holds still
lesson:
Today we work on one thing: how a poem handles time. Time in a poem means when things happen — past, present, or about to happen — and the poem can move between them.

This poem holds still at the start. The cold frame "stands with its lid propped half-up." Nothing moves yet. Then it reaches back to yesterday: "your hands remember weights they carried yesterday." Then it comes forward and starts moving in the present: "Now the hinge decides. The lid goes up."

It works because the long still part makes you wait. When the poem finally says "Now," you feel the wait end. The change from remembering to acting tells you a decision got made.

Try this: hold one moment still for a few lines, then use the word "Now" to start the action.

The second time through, listen for how long the stillness lasts before "So — up!" lands.

Here is the poem.
poem:
The cold frame stands with its lid propped half-up,
the way you left it, undecided, neither open to the frost
nor shut against it—a hinge caught thinking.
Below the glass the last of what you set out breathes slow,
and your hands remember weights they carried yesterday:
stone against stone laid level, the measured count of what
goes in the ground and what gets saved back in its pot,
the long arithmetic of hours that only comes out even
somewhere past the snow. You are not behind. You are
a man who tallies honest and sleeps on it.
Now the hinge decides. The lid goes up, the day comes in.

The small green things you rooted are leaning toward a window you haven't opened yet,

So — up!
